title: Flying with a baby: what to really expect
summary: Little ears, choosing seats, and what the crew can (and can't) do

sections.heading: Little ears
sections.text: Changes in air pressure during take-off and landing can make little ears uncomfortable. A feed, a bottle or a dummy can help, because sucking and swallowing helps balance the pressure. Landing is often the trickier part, so keep something back for the descent.

sections.heading: Choosing seats
list: On long-haul flights, bassinets fix to the bulkhead rows. Ask for one when you book
An aisle seat makes nappy-change trips easier
Babies can't sit in, or right next to, an emergency exit row

sections.heading: Your lap or their own seat?
sections.text: Babies under 2 can usually travel on your lap. The American Academy of Pediatrics says a baby is safest in their own seat in an approved car seat, so if that's an option for you, ask the airline which car seats they accept.

sections.heading: The crew
sections.text: They've seen it all before, and a crying baby is part of flying. Services differ between airlines, though. Ryanair, for example, says it doesn't warm baby bottles, so bring a flask or ready-made milk just in case.

tip.label: Worth remembering
tip.text: The flight is usually easier than the version in your head. And if your baby cries, the American Academy of Pediatrics says to feel free to ignore the stares.
